etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English fat, from Old English fǣtt (“fatted, fat”), from Proto-West Germanic *faitid (“fatted”), originally the past participle of the verb *faitijan (“to make fat”), from *fait (“fat”).

definitions.definition: Carrying more fat than usual on one's body; plump; not lean or thin.

quote.citation: 1932, New Orleans (La.) Board of Health, Vox Sanitatis
quote.text: While Hennessey is pouring the milk, the fat guy with the big pot-belly, will come over and write a lot of junk in his little book.

quote.citation: 1976 September 29, Richard Flaste, “Viewing Childhood As it Is”, in The New York Times‎[1]:
quote.text: […]  Ruth‐ellen Stark and Elizabeth Ryan are about ten times fatter, but even they can't compare to Bruce…”

quote.citation: 2014, Isabel Quintero, Gabi, a Girl in Pieces, Cinco Puntos Press, →ISBN, page 46:
quote.text: Because, really, who would like the fat girl? Sebastian said I was crazy for thinking that.

definitions.definition: Thick; large.

quote.citation: 1861, Charles James Lever, A Day's Ride:
quote.text: The thickest salmon, the curdiest trout, the fattest partridge, and the most tender woodcock smoked on his board, and, rumor said, cooked with a delicacy that more pretentious houses could not rival.

definitions.definition: Bulbous; rotund.

quote.citation: 1908, W[illiam] B[lair] M[orton] Ferguson, chapter IV, in Zollenstein, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: So this was my future home, I thought!  […]  Backed by towering hills, the but faintly discernible purple line of the French boundary off to the southwest, a sky of palest Gobelin flecked with fat, fleecy little clouds, it in truth looked a dear little city; the city of one's dreams.

definitions.definition: Bountiful.
Oily; greasy; unctuous; rich (said of food).
(obsolete) Exhibiting the qualities of a fat animal; coarse; heavy; gross; dull; stupid.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Isaiah 6:10, column 1:
quote.text: Make the heart of this people fat, […]

quote.citation: 1855 July 21, Ralph Waldo Emerson, letter to Walter Whitman
quote.text: making our western wits fat & mean

definitions.definition: Fertile; productive.

quote.citation: 1974, “Which Way Africa”, performed by Tunji Oyelana:
quote.text: Land was fatter, soil was rich, hands were many

definitions.definition: Rich; producing a large income; desirable.

quote.citation: 1882, Thomas Carlyle, Reminiscences:
quote.text: now parson of Troston, a fat living in Suffolk

definitions.definition: Abounding in riches; affluent; fortunate.

quote.citation: , "Why Christ's Doctrine was Rejected"
quote.text: persons grown fat and wealthy by a long and successful imposture

definitions.definition: (dated, printing) Of a character which enables the compositor to make large wages; said of matter containing blank, cuts, or many leads, etc.
(golf) Being a shot in which the ground is struck before the ball.

quote.citation: 1992, DeDe Owens, Linda K. Bunker, Advanced Golf: Steps to Success, page 81:
quote.text: Hitting a thin shot from a fairway bunker is more productive than hitting a fat shot.

definitions.definition: (theater) Of a role: significant; major; meaty.

quote.citation: 1965, Edmund Fuller, A Pageant of the Theatre, page 131:
quote.text: He is what the theatre calls a “fat” role — a man suddenly confronted by a terrible duty. He is called upon to revenge the murder of his father and to right a wrong against the state.

quote.citation: 1997, Harold Clurman, On Directing, page 12:
quote.text: He seeks a fat role in a hit show, lest he diminish his market value.

quote.citation: 2012, Greg Robinson, Larry S. Tajiri, Pacific Citizens, page 9:
quote.text: Joe Hirakawa, formerly of the Seattle Civic Repertory Theatre, was a waterfront peddler in “Madame Butterfly” and had a fat role in “Beauty Parlor,” an indie.

definitions.definition: (slang) Being greatly or substantially such; real.

quote.citation: 1970-1975, Lou Sullivan, personal diary, quoted in 2019, Ellis Martin, Zach Ozma (editors), We Both Laughed In Pleasure
quote.text: I'd've liked to hang around but the guys were in a fat hurry.

definitions.definition: (computing) Carrying additional data or functionality.
Alternative form of phat

quote.citation: 2011, Joe Shambro, How to Start a Home-based DJ Business, page 19:
quote.text: This isn't a place to talk about “hitting the decks” and making “fat beats”—you're not selling to an industry peer.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English fat, fatt, fatte, from the adjective above, and possibly from Old English fǣt (“fat”, recorded once), from Proto-West Germanic *fait, from Proto-Germanic *faitą, *faitaz (“fat”).

definitions.definition: Such tissue as food: the fatty portion of (or trimmings from) meat cuts.
(uncountable) A specialized animal tissue with high lipid content, used for long-term storage of energy: fat tissue.

(countable) A lipid that is solid at room temperature, which fat tissue contains and which is also found in the blood circulation; sometimes, a refined substance chemically resembling such naturally occurring lipids.

quote.citation: 2018, Kristin Lawless, Formerly known as food, →ISBN, page 32:
quote.text: In fact, the fats that are most stable and least likely to oxidize with heat are the highly saturated fats we've long been told to avoid—lard, tallow, butter, and coconut and palm oils.

definitions.definition: That part of an organization deemed wasteful.
(slang) An erection.
(golf) A poorly played shot where the ball is struck by the top part of the club head. (see also thin, shank, toe)
The best or richest productions; the best part.
(dated, printing) Work containing much blank, or its equivalent, and therefore profitable to the compositor.
(informal, derogatory) A fat person.

quote.citation: 1996, Roger Stone, "Local Swing Fever", highlighted by National Enquirer in September 1996 and Daily Mail in January 2019
quote.text: Prefer military, bodybuilders, jocks. No smokers or fats please.

definitions.definition: A beef cattle fattened for sale.

quote.citation: 1934, Henry G. Lamond, An Aviary On The Plains, page 7:
quote.text: Before riding over to the fats we'll have a look about us.

definitions.definition: (transitive, archaic) To make fat; to fatten.
(intransitive, archaic) To become fat; to fatten.
(transitive, golf) To hit (a golf ball) with a fat shot.

quote.citation: 2019 April 2, Rick Reilly, How and why President Trump cheats at golf — even when he’s playing against Tiger Woods‎[2], archived from the original on 2022-03-29:
quote.text: “On this one hole, Donald hits his second and fats it into the water,” Faxon remembers. “But he quickly says to me, ‘Hey, throw me another ball; they weren’t looking.’ So I do. But he fats that one into the water, too. So he drives up and drops where he should’ve dropped the first time and hits it on the green.”

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English fat, from Old English fæt (“vat, vessel, jar, cup, casket, division”), from Proto-Germanic *fatą (“vessel”), from Proto-Indo-European *pod- (“vessel”). Cognate with Dutch vat (“barrel, vessel”), German Fass (“barrel, drum”), Swedish fat (“barrel, dish, cask”). See vat.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A large tub or vessel for water, wine, or other liquids; a cistern.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Joel 2:24, column 1:
quote.text: And the floores ſhall bee full of wheate, and the fats ſhall ouerflowe with wine and oyle.

quote.citation: 1882, James Edwin Thorold Rogers, A History of Agriculture and Prices in England, volume 4, page 429:
quote.text: In 1431 New College purchases brewing vessels, under the names of a mash fat, for 6s. 10d., a wort fat for 2s., a 'Gilleding' tub for 2s. 6d., and two tunning barrels at 8d. each, a leaden boiler for 24s., another for 12s., and a great copper beer pot for 13s. 4d.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A dry measure, generally equal to nine bushels.
